title: Messy data in, clean records out: RecordScrub, a data-cleaning API
author: DSP
summary: Every project eventually inherits the same spreadsheet: emails in three different cases, phone numbers formatted six ways, names like "DOE, john michael", and the same customer entered twice. Cleaning it by hand, or with a pile of regexes you don't quite trust, is nobody's favorite afternoon. RecordScrub is a small API we built at DSP to do that job in one call. It's live on RapidAPI now, with a free tier. What it does Email validation & normalization , single or batch, with valid/invalid stats and a plain-language reason for every rejection Phone normalization to E.164 , powered by Google's libphonenumber, so (312) 555-0142 becomes +13125550142 Name normalization , "DOE, john michael" → John Michael Doe , with first/last split out US address normalization , state codes, ZIP+4, standardized street suffixes Batch record cleaning , send CSV-style records, get snake_case keys, per-field cleaning, and exact dedupe on the fields you choose, with a duplicate report showing what was dropped and why Every dropped or altered value comes back with a _warnings explanation. No silent data loss. A taste curl -X POST https://record-scrub.p.rapidapi.com/v1/normalize/phone \ -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: YOUR_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"phone": "(312) 555-0142"}' { "original" : "(312) 555-0142" , "normalized" : "+13125550142" , "valid" : true , "country_code" : 1 , "national_format" : "(312) 555-0142" } And the batch cleaner, deduplicating on email + phone: { "records" : [{ "name" : "John Doe" , "email" : "john@example.com" , "phone" : "+13125550142" }], "stats" : { "received" : 2 , "returned" : 1 , "duplicates_removed" : 1 }, "duplicates" : [{ "index" : 1 , "duplicate_of" : 0 , "record" : { "..." : "..." }}]} How it's built FastAPI, completely stateless. Requests are processed in transit and nothing is stored , so there's no database to leak from. It runs on a free-tier host, so the first call after a quiet spell can take a few extra seconds while it wakes up; after that it's fast. Pricing Every endpoint is available on every plan, including the free tier. No feature gates, no Pro-only cleaners, no endpoint held back to force an upgrade. Upgrading simply gets you more requests per month: start free with 100 requests a month, move up to Pro at $10/month for 5,000, and scale from there if your batch volume grows. You pay for volume, not for access. Try it: https://rapidapi.com/darksundarker/api/record-scrub Feedback very welcome, especially the "I wish it also cleaned X" kind. That's how the v2 list gets written.

title: Owe: Gemma 4 drafts the reply I kept avoiding, then a local check decides if I can send it
author: Aroso Emmanuel
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Owe pastes the message you have been avoiding. Gemma 4 ( gemma-4-26b-a4b-it , via the Gemini API) drafts a reply of at most 60 words, names the one fact it must not invent, and says whether you can send it. owe/guard.py then runs locally and can override that answer. A number, email, or name that was not in the message keeps the reply unsent. The message is sent to the Gemini API. This does not run offline. The send decision stays on the machine. Demo Message: "Hey — are you still coming Saturday? Priya said you might bring the speaker. Let me know by tonight, otherwise I'll ask Jordan." With no decision supplied, Gemma took 63.6 seconds and returned a 10-word holding reply: "I haven't decided yet. I'll let you know by tonight." It named the missing fact (whether you are coming, and whether you have the speaker) and can_send was true, because the reply adds no plan. With a note, "I can't come Saturday, but I can drop the speaker with Priya tonight," the reply was that sentence and nothing more (32.4 seconds). The model copied the instructions into the missing-fact field, and the guard replaced that line. The guard's job is the invented reply "Yes, I will be there at 7 with the speaker." The digit 7 is not in the message. tests/test_guard.py runs that case through the same function the CLI uses, and can_send comes back false. Nine tests, no API calls. python -m owe examples/saturday.txt How I Built It Gemma returns one JSON object at temperature 0.2: reply, must_not_invent, can_send, why. No system instruction. Transient 429, 500, and 503 responses are retried. review() then checks word count (1 to 60), numbers, emails, and capitalized names against the message and the optional note. That limit came from two DEV posts. Slothshot kept a name only when the words were really on the screen. Gemma 4 on 16GB showed short structured prompts holding together. Owe asks for three short fields, then checks them in code. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? gemma-4-26b-a4b-it is open-weight. Calling it through the Gemini API is allowed for Best Use of Gemma, and it means the message leaves the laptop. The open part I control is the function after the call: a closed assistant will often invent the yes, the time, and the promise. This one can be told no by local code. Swapping the Gemma endpoint does not change owe/guard.py . The Lazy Payoff The work skipped is composing the holding reply. 63.6 seconds, 10 words, and the name of the decision still left open. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: the project does not work without gemma-4-26b-a4b-it . The local check stops an invented reply from being marked sendable. title: Python Dataclasses vs Pydantic: Benchmarked, Then Decided
author: Muhammad Saud
summary: Dataclasses and Pydantic both let you define structured data in Python, but they solve different problems. A dataclass is a lightweight container for data your code already trusts, while Pydantic is a validation layer for data coming from outside your code. Choosing wrong costs you either safety or speed, so this guide benchmarks both and gives you a decision rule you can apply in a minute. Key takeaways Use Pydantic at the boundary where untrusted data enters: API requests, config files, webhook payloads. Use dataclasses inside your code, where the data is already validated and you want the fastest, simplest container. Measured on Python 3.12 with Pydantic 2.14.1, Pydantic construction costs about 2.8 microseconds per object versus 0.5 for a dataclass, roughly five times slower. Pydantic serialises faster than dataclasses: model_dump took 3.2 microseconds against 6.6 for dataclasses.asdict in the same test. attrs sits between the two: as fast as a dataclass, with validators and converters if you want them. At web-request scale the difference is noise; at millions of rows per second it decides the design. What does each one actually do? A dataclass, in the standard library since Python 3.7, is a class decorator that writes the boring methods for you: init , repr , eq . It adds no validation at all. If you pass a string where a float belongs, it stores the string and says nothing. That is not a bug; it is the design. A dataclass trusts its caller. Pydantic is a validation library. Its BaseModel checks every field when an object is created, coerces compatible types (the string "129.99" becomes the float 129.99), and raises a detailed ValidationError when the data does not fit. Pydantic v2, released in June 2023, is built on pydantic-core, a Rust validation engine. The Pydantic team claims v2 is 5 to 50 times faster than v1; that is their own benchmark, not an independent one, and it compares v2 against v1, not against dataclasses. Here is the same order record in both styles: from dataclasses import dataclass, field from pydantic import BaseModel @dataclass class Order: order_id: int customer: str total: float currency: str = "EUR" class OrderModel(BaseModel): order_id: int customer: str total: float currency: str = "EUR" A dataclass trusts you. This runs fine and stores a string in total . Order(order_id=1, customer="Ada", total="not-a-number") Pydantic does not. This raises ValidationError. OrderModel(order_id=1, customer="Ada", total="not-a-number") That single difference drives the whole decision. Everything else, speed, ergonomics, ecosystem, is secondary. How fast is Pydantic really? Most articles on this topic quote the Pydantic team's own numbers. I ran the comparison myself instead, on Python 3.12.3 with Pydantic 2.14.1 and attrs 26.1.0, using a seven-field order model with a nested address. Each figure is the best of five runs of 20,000 operations, in microseconds per operation. OperationDataclassattrsPydantic v2Construct from typed values0.520.482.77Parse from a raw dict1.45*—3.68Parse from a JSON string——9.93Serialise to a dict6.595.593.22Serialise to JSON11.87—3.34 *The dataclass dict figure is a manual unpack with no validation at all, so it is not a like-for-like comparison. It is there to show what skipping validation buys you: about 2 microseconds. Two findings matter. First, Pydantic construction is roughly five times slower than a dataclass, 2.77 versus 0.52 microseconds. If you parse a million rows, that is about 2.8 seconds against 0.5 seconds. Real, but only decisive at bulk scale. Second, Pydantic is faster at serialisation. Its model_dump() took 3.22 microseconds against 6.59 for dataclasses.asdict(), and model_dump_json() took 3.34 against 11.87 for the asdict-plus-json.dumps route. The dataclass helper is recursive and slow; Pydantic serialises through its Rust core. So the common claim that Pydantic is "slower" is only half true: it costs more to build, less to dump. Keep the scale in mind. A typical web request spends milliseconds on the database and the network. Two extra microseconds of validation per object is invisible there. It only becomes a design constraint in ETL jobs, log pipelines, and event streams that construct millions of objects per second. When should you use dataclasses? Use dataclasses for data that your own code creates and controls: internal domain objects, the results of a calculation, values passed between your own functions. There is nothing to validate because you built the values yourself, and the standard library dependency means zero install cost and zero version risk. Dataclasses are also the right pick when your objects are short-lived and numerous, for example rows in a hot loop that you have already parsed once. from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(frozen=True) class Money: amount: float currency: str = "EUR" def __add__(self, other: "Money") -> "Money": if other.currency != self.currency: raise ValueError("cannot add different currencies") return Money(self.amount + other.amount, self.currency) Frozen dataclasses give you immutability for free, which makes them safe to share between threads and to use as dictionary keys once all fields are hashable. If you need a little more, slots=True cuts memory use, and field(default_factory=list) handles mutable defaults safely. When is Pydantic the right call? Use Pydantic wherever data crosses a trust boundary: HTTP request bodies, CLI arguments, environment config, webhook payloads, rows read from a CSV you did not produce. FastAPI is built on Pydantic for exactly this reason: your endpoint declares a model and invalid requests are rejected before your code runs. Pydantic also shines for configuration, where a wrong type in an environment variable should fail loudly at startup instead of silently corrupting behaviour hours later. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings class Settings(BaseSettings): database_url: str max_retries: int = Field(default=3, ge=0, le=10) debug: bool = False try: settings = Settings() # reads env vars, validates types and ranges except ValidationError as exc: print(exc) # every bad field listed, with a path and a message Pydantic's error messages are the feature people underestimate. A ValidationError lists every failing field with its location and a human-readable reason, which is far more useful in a log than a bare TypeError three functions deep. If you want the validation without the coercion, strict mode (model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)) rejects "129.99" as a float instead of converting it. What about attrs? attrs is the third option and the oldest of the three. It predates dataclasses and inspired them. In my benchmark it was the fastest constructor at 0.48 microseconds, and it offers optional validators and converters, so it covers the middle ground: dataclass speed with opt-in validation. The catch is that its validation is per-field and manual, nothing like Pydantic's schema-driven parsing, and the ecosystem around it is smaller. Pick attrs when you want dataclass ergonomics with a few validators and you do not need JSON schema generation or FastAPI integration. For most teams, though, the choice is binary: dataclasses or Pydantic, and attrs is a specialist tool. How do you decide in practice? Apply one rule: validate at the boundary, use plain containers inside. Your API handler, your config loader, and your file importer take Pydantic models. The moment the data is validated, convert it to a dataclass or a plain object and pass that around internally. This is the pattern FastAPI itself encourages, and it gives you both guarantees: bad data is rejected early, and your hot paths pay no validation tax. Boundary: Pydantic validates the incoming request. class CreateOrderRequest(BaseModel): order_id: int customer: str total: float Inside: a dataclass carries the validated data. @dataclass(frozen=True) class Order: order_id: int customer: str total: float def handle(payload: dict) -> Order: req = CreateOrderRequest.model_validate(payload) # raises on bad data return Order(req.order_id, req.customer, req.total) There is one exception. If your whole application is a thin wrapper around validated data, a small API with a handful of endpoints, keeping Pydantic models everywhere is simpler than converting back and forth, and the performance cost is negligible. Do not build a conversion layer you do not need. What is still unknown? My numbers come from one small model on one machine; a model with fifty fields, heavy use of unions, or deeply nested lists will shift the ratios, and Pydantic's relative cost grows with validation complexity. The Pydantic team's 5 to 50 times claim about v2 versus v1 is their own measurement and I have not independently reproduced it. Finally, Pydantic v2 is a separate install with its own release cadence, so pin it in production and check the changelog before upgrading, the v1 to v2 migration changed several behaviours. Conclusion Dataclasses and Pydantic are not rivals. A dataclass is the fastest way to hold data you trust; Pydantic is the most reliable way to accept data you do not. Measure your own workload if you parse at bulk scale, but for most applications the decision is architectural, not numerical: put Pydantic at the boundary, dataclasses inside, and let each do the job it was built for. title: A live call coach with two modes: interviews and meetings
author: Made by Asking
summary: Try the UI demo in the browser, no install: https://henrylop.github.io/live-call-coach/ui/ Interview mode In an interview, the right example is somewhere in your head and it surfaces five minutes late. live-call-coach is a small package that listens to the other side of a call and shows tiered hints while the question is still fresh. The quick tier answers in about 1.5 seconds with an opening line, three key points and a hard-question flag. The deep tier is grounded in your own notes and cites them. When a new question starts before a card is ready, the stale card is dropped. The whole pipeline runs on a simulated clock, so replays are instant and the tests are deterministic. There is a UI demo in ui/ that needs no server: open index.html and watch a scripted interview play through. The demo and the tests use an offline stub, so nothing here calls a paid API. Meeting mode Work calls ask for facts you own but cannot look up in the moment. live-call-coach has a meeting mode for that: for each question it builds a card with a line to say and the facts behind it, with their sources, and it keeps a running ledger of commitments (who, what, when). Two details carry most of the design. A card that is still being built when the next question starts is dropped rather than shown late. And the reader that follows the call is read-only: it has an allow-list with one entry, turning on captions, and a test scans the source for anything that types or sends. The UI demo in ui/ replays an invented call with no server, so you can see the cards arrive, a stale card leave and the ledger fill. The code runs offline against a stub model. title: Compress and Convert Thousands of Images in Your Browser—No Installation Needed🚀
author: Ethan Carter
summary: A folder of 500 product photos shouldn't mean 500 separate trips through an image compressor. Neither should 600 screenshots or 1,000 images for a website migration mean installing a desktop application just to prepare the files. I built CompressFly to make image compression and format conversion available directly in the browser, including batches that run into thousands of images. The important engineering decision is how the application manages work and memory. It doesn't need to keep every image fully decoded at the same time. It processes a limited number of images, releases their temporary processing resources, and keeps taking work from the queue. 500, 600, and 1,000 are examples of batch sizes, not preset limits. I also tested 1,000 images in each of two batch runs: JPG compression and conversion to WebP. The current image selection and scheduling flow doesn't impose a fixed image-count ceiling. The practical limit still depends on image dimensions, formats, browser resources, and the device doing the work. Bulk image compression without installing software For everyday image preparation, the browser can now provide the whole workflow: select local files, compress or convert them on the device, then download the results. In CompressFly, you can choose multiple images, select a folder where supported, or drag files into the page. You apply settings to the batch instead of opening and exporting each file separately. For example: Image collection Batch job 500 JPG product photos Reduce file sizes before adding them to a store 600 PNG screenshots Compress them, or convert suitable assets to WebP 1,000 mixed JPG and PNG images Prepare a consistent output format for a site migration 2,000 existing WebP images Run another compression pass when different settings suit the destination These are workflow examples, not benchmark results or guaranteed completion counts for every device. A folder containing 2,000 small web images is a different workload from 2,000 full-resolution camera photos. Why a batch of 1,000 images doesn't need 1,000 active tasks The browser's File API lets a web application read files the user selects. Selecting a folder doesn't require the application to immediately decode every image into pixels. That distinction matters because a compressed file and its decoded image have very different memory requirements. Consider the 3680 × 2066 dimensions used in my tests. A single RGBA pixel buffer requires: 3680 × 2066 × 4 bytes = 30,411,520 bytes , or roughly 29 MiB. That is one buffer for one image, before accounting for decoder memory, encoder workspaces, previews, and the output. Keeping 1,000 buffers of that size at once would require about 28.3 GiB just for those buffers, exceeding this computer's 16 GB of memory. This is a theoretical buffer-size calculation, not a measurement of the application's actual memory use. CompressFly uses a queue with limited concurrency. A few tasks run while the remaining files wait. When one task finishes, its slot becomes available and the next image starts. A slower image occupies its own slot; other slots can continue moving through the batch. The queue can contain 500, 600, 1,000, or more files without requiring that many decoders to run together. Conceptual illustration: 1,000 queued images is an example, not a batch limit. Finish an image, release its working resources, continue Limiting concurrency controls the number of active tasks. Cleaning up after each image prevents completed tasks from unnecessarily keeping their processing resources alive. In the image-processing paths I reviewed, workers used for encoding or conversion are terminated after returning their results. Worker references are cleared, and temporary object URLs are revoked where those URLs are created for the processing operation. Relevant paths also transfer buffers to workers instead of copying them unnecessarily. The cycle is straightforward: Take the next image from the queue. Decode it and perform the requested compression or conversion. Keep the output needed for preview or download. Release the task's temporary processing resources and free its queue slot. Start the next waiting image. That is what makes a batch of thousands practical: the application keeps moving through the collection instead of accumulating thousands of active image-processing workspaces. There is an important boundary here. Releasing working resources doesn't mean the batch uses zero memory. The page still keeps file references, previews, and completed outputs needed for downloads. The browser also controls when eligible JavaScript memory is reclaimed. Per-image cleanup reduces processing pressure; it doesn't promise unlimited total capacity. Web Workers keep heavy processing away from the interface Web Workers run scripts in background threads. CompressFly uses worker-based processing paths for its image operations, so substantial encoding and conversion work can happen away from the page's main thread. This gives the interface room to display progress and individual results while the queue advances. It doesn't make processing free: the CPU and memory still belong to the user's device. Each image also has its own processing status. An individual failure can be recorded while the scheduler continues with other queued files. For a large batch, that is more useful than treating one unsupported or damaged image as the failure of the entire collection. Tested: 1,000 images on a 13-inch M2 MacBook Pro I ran both tests on my 13-inch MacBook Pro (M2, 2022) . Here is the hardware configuration and the input used for each run: Test detail Configuration Computer 13-inch MacBook Pro, 2022 Chip Apple M2 CPU 8 cores Memory 16 GB unified memory Images per run 1,000 JPG files Size of each source file 5.51 MB, as displayed in the tool Dimensions of each source image 3680 × 2066 pixels These were two separate batch operations, each containing 1,000 files. The source files shared the size and dimensions listed above; this wasn't a test across 1,000 different image sizes or formats. JPG compression: 1,000 out of 1,000 completed With image quality set to 85% , and Keep metadata and Lossless unchecked, the compressor reported Compressed 1000/1000 . The visible sample results went from 5.51 MB to 889.06 KB per image , a displayed reduction of 84.24% , while retaining 3680 × 2066 dimensions. The batch summary reported 4.53 GB reduced (84%) . These figures are the tool's displayed values, including its rounding. My compression test: 1,000 JPG images completed in one batch on the M2 MacBook Pro. JPG to WebP: 1,000 out of 1,000 completed For the conversion test, I selected WebP output and 90% image quality. The converter reported Converted 1000/1000 . title: Node.js Commerce Watch Parties: Host Authority With Durable Notification Recovery
author: DorianReed2186
summary: A single authoritative host is the practical default for a Node.js commerce watch party. Let that host publish playback position and timed product-drop events; let viewers follow rather than vote. Peer consensus survives host loss more elegantly, but it adds election, split-brain, ordering, and reconciliation work to a feature whose honest promise is approximate synchronization. Short answer: choose host authority, make departure a named state transition, and keep notifications for offline shoppers in a durable queue or outbox. The socket is delivery, not storage. Tell viewers that playback may drift instead of implying frame-perfect sync. Infrai fits one specific part of this design: a small team can put the durable queue and realtime publish contract behind the same API key, then inspect both contracts through public discovery before writing the worker. It does not decide playback authority for the application. This experiment is constrained by delivery guarantees at fan-out, not by the prettiest SDK. A product reveal sent to 8,000 viewers has two different obligations: connected viewers should see it quickly, while disconnected viewers must not lose it. Treating one transient publish as both obligations is the simple design that fails. Two obligations. Two mechanisms. Should a watch party use an authoritative host or peer consensus for playback? Consensus sounds fair because no participant is special. It also forces the application to answer questions that host authority deletes: Which clock wins? How many peers form a quorum after a mobile network split? Can a late tab overturn a newer seek? What happens when two partitions each elect a leader? WebRTC defines browser real-time communication primitives; it does not supply the application-level consensus protocol for a watch party. One source removes almost all of that machinery. The host emits a monotonically increasing event sequence with its media position and a server timestamp. A viewer applies only a newer sequence. Product notifications refer to that same sequence, so a "buy now" prompt cannot legitimately precede the scene that introduces it. The trade-off is blunt. If the host disappears, authority disappears too. Handle that event explicitly: pause authoritative product-drop publication, appoint a replacement under a documented policy, then resume from the last accepted sequence. Do not quietly turn every viewer into an authority. Perfect synchronization is unavailable. Say that in the interface. "Synced to host" and "Reconnecting" are defensible states; a promise that every display is on the same frame is not. That wording matters. The fan-out boundary decides the real operating bill The useful cost model starts with workload shape: concurrent viewers, events per minute, reconnect frequency, offline duration, retained notifications, and duplicate-processing rate. Vendor unit prices are only one input. Engineering time spent joining identity, retry semantics, credentials, logs, and invoices belongs in the bill too. So does downstream damage from showing a product prompt twice or dropping it entirely. Count the glue. For online delivery, a realtime channel is enough. For an absent shopper, the notification must become a durable message before the live publish is attempted. A worker can later deliver it in order, and its consumer must be idempotent because standard queues are at-least-once. Use a stable event ID such as drop_1042 , store the last applied playback sequence per viewer, and make duplicate receipt a no-op. This is where Infrai is an interesting fit, rather than an automatic winner. Its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so evaluating a new operation is one discovery read instead of an SDK adoption. The same key covers realtime and queue capabilities; that can reduce credential and invoice glue around the online/offline handoff. The platform reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is less important here than a consistent contract at this exact boundary. I would try Infrai for a small team that needs realtime fan-out plus durable offline notification handling under one credential, because the self-describing contract reduces integration work at the boundary where messages are commonly lost. The supporting advantage is operational: one key and one bill replace separate credential rotation and reconciliation for these two capabilities. The cost is concentration. One vendor becomes one trust boundary, one bill, and one shared dependency. A focused Node.js contract check Do not guess a queue or publish payload from a product description. The discovery response supplies the method, path, full request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. This TypeScript program fetches that contract, selects the two capabilities at the handoff, and prints their actual paths and examples before any integration code is written. type Capability = { id : string ; module : string ; method : string ; path : string ; available : boolean ; idempotent ?: boolean ; params ?: unknown ; examples ?: unknown ; }; type Discovery = { version : string ; generated_at : string ; capabilities : Capability []; }; const apiKey = process . env . INFRAI_API_KEY ; if ( ! apiKey ) throw new Error ( " INFRAI_API_KEY is required " ); async function loadContracts (): Promise < void > { const response = await fetch ( " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery " , { method : " GET " , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ apiKey } ` , }, }); if ( response . status === 429 ) { const retryAfter = Number ( response . headers . get ( " retry-after " )); const delayMs = Number . isFinite ( retryAfter ) ? retryAfter * 1 _000 : 1 _000 ; await new Promise (( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , delayMs )); return loadContracts (); } if ( ! response . ok ) { const reason = await response . text (); throw new Error ( `Discovery failed ( ${ response . status } ): ${ reason } ` ); } const discovery = ( await response . json ()) as Discovery ; const selected = discovery . capabilities . filter ( ( capability ) => capability . path === " /v1/realtime/publish " || capability . module === " queue " , ); if ( ! selected . some (( capability ) => capability . path === " /v1/realtime/publish " )) { throw new Error ( " Realtime publish contract was not discovered " ); } console . log ( JSON . stringify ( selected , null , 2 )); } await loadContracts (); Discovery is public and does not require a key; the sample still supplies the same INFRAI_API_KEY that the subsequent queue and publish calls use as Authorization: Bearer <key> . Write retries use a stable Idempotency-Key . Select paths from the returned path fields and start from the runnable TypeScript examples. That keeps the code tied to the live schema instead of a hand-written route guess. The handoff itself has one invariant: durable acceptance happens before realtime publication. A production worker acknowledges its queue message only after publication succeeds, while each client records eventId and playbackSequence before rendering. Those checks cover different duplicates: redelivery at the worker and replay or reconnect at the viewer. How do the real alternatives differ? Pusher Channels is a focused hosted pub/sub choice. Pairing it with Amazon SQS gives a familiar division between online fan-out and durable work, but it requires two signups, two credential sets, two billing relationships, and glue that maps an SQS message to a Pusher event. That separation can be desirable when independent vendor boundaries matter more than integration overhead. Ably also specializes in realtime messaging and documents channel behavior. It is a sound direction when the realtime layer needs a specialist and the team accepts a separate queue or outbox contract for offline business notifications. LiveKit is centered on realtime media and data in rooms; it deserves a close look when audio/video transport, participants, and room control dominate the project, though the application must still decide who controls playback and where absent-user notifications persist. Socket.IO is different again: it is a library and protocol you can operate within your Node.js system. It offers control and avoids handing the whole realtime tier to a hosted service, in exchange for owning deployment, scaling, presence behavior, and the durable-message connection yourself. These are meaningful differences, not logo choices: the first decision is whether the team wants an integrated API, a realtime specialist joined to a queue, a media-room platform, or infrastructure it operates directly. Pick the ownership model first. Stack Best fit Delivery boundary to own Operational trade-off Infrai realtime plus queue capabilities Small team minimizing integration surfaces Idempotent worker-to-publish handoff One credential and contract; one shared vendor dependency Pusher Channels plus Amazon SQS Teams preferring specialized services SQS consumer, Pusher publisher, and identity mapping Two signups, credential sets, bills, and explicit glue Ably plus a durable queue Realtime behavior needs a specialist platform Queue retention and replay into channels Separate offline-message lifecycle LiveKit plus an outbox Media rooms are the center of the product Room data versus durable commerce events Media-oriented system plus a persistence layer Socket.IO plus a queue Teams that want infrastructure control Scaling, presence, replay, and persistence More operations owned by the application team No row wins in the abstract. The smallest credible design depends on what failure you are willing to own. For an indie product, host authority plus an explicit durable handoff is usually tractable. For a team already operating AWS, the separate Pusher-and-SQS shape may justify its extra glue. For a media-heavy experience, LiveKit can be the better center of gravity. A team willing to run its own realtime infrastructure may prefer Socket.IO. What should you measure before copying this design? Measure the workload, not a demo. Record connected viewers per party, publish attempts per event, 429 retries, reconnects, duplicate deliveries rejected, queue age at successful fan-out, and the interval between host departure and restored authority. Track the percentage of product notifications that reach an online client and the percentage later recovered for an offline client as separate numbers. Mixing them hides the precise failure this architecture is meant to prevent. Also test ugly state transitions: the host closes a laptop during a product drop; replacement authority starts while an older event is in flight; a viewer reconnects with a stale sequence; the worker stops after publish but before acknowledgement. Each test needs an observable expected state. None requires peer consensus if the authority rule and idempotency contract are explicit. The nastiest sequence is longer. The queue accepts drop_1042 ; the worker publishes it; the host leaves before the worker acknowledges; a replacement resumes from playback sequence 381; then the worker receives the same queue item again. The correct result is still one visible prompt. The worker reuses the stable idempotency key, the viewer rejects an already-recorded event ID, and the replacement host cannot move playback backward because clients reject an older sequence. This is why delivery guarantees at fan-out need several small contracts rather than one vague claim of reliability. Keep the promise modest. A watch party can coordinate playback and product prompts without claiming perfect sync. Host authority keeps the steady state understandable; durable notification storage protects the shopper who was absent; a deliberate succession policy covers the one failure authority introduces. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema and runnable example for each capability before wiring it into the worker. References W3C WebRTC 1.0 Pusher Channels documentation Amazon SQS developer guide Ably documentation LiveKit documentation Socket.IO documentation Infrai official documentation

title: RAG reranking: Boosting Precision in Production Systems
author: Imversion Tech
summary: What RAG reranking does in a production pipeline If your RAG system retrieves something relevant but still answers poorly, the problem is often ranking. The right evidence exists, but it is buried under chunks that look similar and read well enough to confuse the generator. RAG reranking exists for that exact failure mode. Table of Contents What RAG reranking does in a production pipeline RAG reranking Key Takeaways Where RAG reranking sits in a two-stage retrieval pipeline Cross-encoder reranking vs top-k retrieval alone How RAG reranking changes precision, recall, latency, and cost Precision goes up first Recall depends on the candidate pool Latency and cost rise with every extra candidate When top-k retrieval is enough without a retrieval reranker How to benchmark whether RAG reranking earns its cost Build the comparison Run an experiment matrix Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a cross-encoder and a bi-encoder in retrieval systems? How does RAG reranking affect hallucination risk? Why should I benchmark RAG reranking separately from the LLM? When is RAG reranking usually not worth the cost? Should reranking score full documents or chunks? RAG reranking sits between retrieval and generation in a production RAG pipeline, where it reorders the first-pass results with a more precise relevance model. Most often, that means cross-encoder reranking over the top-k candidates. The payoff is better evidence at the top -- with extra latency and inference cost. In a two-stage retrieval flow, the fast layer does recall: BM25, FAISS, Pinecone, or hybrid search pulls a candidate set. Then the retrieval reranker scores each query-passage pair and promotes the passages most likely to answer the question directly. Because a cross-encoder reads both texts together, it catches mismatches that vector similarity often misses -- negation, exact entity alignment, and intent. But reranking is not a default requirement. If top-k retrieval already places the right chunks near the top, adding a reranker may just slow the system down. And rerankers cannot recover documents never retrieved, so a weak candidate set stays weak. At Imversion Technologies Pvt Ltd, the practical view is simple: decisions should be backed by data. Benchmark it with Precision@k, MRR, answer quality, and end-to-end latency before paying the extra cost. RAG reranking Key Takeaways In a two-stage retrieval pipeline, RAG reranking sits after fast first-pass retrieval -- BM25, dense vectors, or hybrid search -- and before the LLM. The flow is simple: retrieve top-k, rerank, then send only the best top-n passages to generation. Cross-encoder reranking improves top-of-list precision because it scores the query and passage together, not independently. That usually helps with hard relevance cases -- negation, intent, entity overlap, and temporal constraints -- where embedding similarity alone can look “close enough” but still rank the wrong chunk first. But rerankers do not fix missed retrieval. They only reorder the candidate set they receive. If the right document never enters top-k, no model-based reranking stage can recover it. So the first retriever still owns recall. Top-k retrieval alone is often enough when the corpus is small, queries are narrow, or baseline metrics already show strong Precision@k and MRR without answer-quality drift. Clarity is better than complexity. Benchmark cross-encoder reranking like an added production dependency: compare answer quality, Precision@k or MRR, latency, and cost at candidate sizes such as top-20 versus top-100. If the gain is small, skip the extra stage. Where RAG reranking sits in a two-stage retrieval pipeline A lot of retrieval problems are really handoff problems. The retriever finds enough material, but the generator receives the wrong few chunks, which means the final answer is shaped by evidence that is merely adjacent instead of actually useful. This is where reranking belongs. Reranking should run after fast first-pass retrieval and before context packing for the LLM. That placement is the whole point of a two-stage retrieval design: stage one casts a wide net cheaply, stage two spends more compute to improve the order of what was found. The full production RAG pipeline usually looks like this: user query intake, optional query rewriting, first-stage retrieval, candidate collection, reranker scoring, top-n context selection, then answer generation. First-stage retrieval is built for recall and speed -- BM25 in Elasticsearch, dense retrieval over FAISS, or hybrid search that combines both. It returns a top-k set of candidate chunks or documents. Then the retrieval reranker takes over. A cross-encoder reranking model does not search the whole corpus. It only sees the query plus each retrieved candidate, scored one pair at a time. So its input is: the normalized user query and the retrieved top-k passages. Its output is: the same candidates, reordered by a stronger relevance score, often with low-value items pushed down. Nothing more. If the right passage never made it into top-k, the reranker cannot rescue it. That boundary matters. A simple example makes the handoff clear. Query: “How do I cancel an annual subscription and will I get a refund?” A first-pass retriever using BM25 or dense retrieval may pull top-50 chunks covering cancellation steps, refund policy, billing FAQs, and even account upgrade docs. Useful, but noisy. The reranker then scores those 50 candidates against the full query and promotes the chunks that directly answer both cancellation and refund . From there, the pipeline packs the best top-5 or top-8 chunks into the LLM context window. Treat reranking as a precision layer, not a retrieval replacement. That framing prevents a common mistake. Teams expect reranking to compensate for weak retrieval, but it cannot do that. If first-stage retrieval is weak, fix candidate generation first -- query rewriting, chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, or a larger top-k. Understanding why the pipeline misses relevant evidence is essential, because reranking improves ranking quality at the top, while recall is still decided upstream. Cross-encoder reranking vs top-k retrieval alone The tradeoff here is simple: top-k retrieval is built to find enough candidates fast, while reranking is built to decide which of those candidates deserve to be seen first. If your current setup already puts the exact supporting passage near rank 1, reranking may be unnecessary. If it does not, this is usually the next thing to test. Top-k retrieval alone is often good enough to find related text. It is not always good enough to put the best evidence first. That gap is exactly where cross-encoder reranking earns its keep in a production RAG pipeline. A bi-encoder retriever -- common in FAISS, Pinecone, Elasticsearch dense search, or SentenceTransformers setups -- encodes the query and each document independently, then compares them with vector similarity. Fast. Scalable. But blunt. It decides relevance from two standalone embeddings, so subtle constraints can get blurred. A cross-encoder does the opposite. It reads the query-document pair together and produces a single relevance score through joint attention, or pairwise scoring in practical terms. That lets model-based reranking catch details first-stage retrieval often misses: negation, entity disambiguation, time filters, and narrow intent. Example: a user asks for “subscription cancellation steps, not refund policy.” Vector retrieval may surface chunks about billing, refunds, and account settings because they are semantically nearby. A cross-encoder reranking layer can push the exact cancellation instructions above merely related policy text. That improves precision at the top -- the part the generator actually sees. There is still a hard boundary: rerankers cannot rescue documents that never entered the candidate set. If top-k is too small, RAG reranking may improve ordering while hurting effective recall. So benchmark the full chain, not the reranker in isolation. Decisions should be backed by data -- Precision@k, MRR, grounded answer quality, latency per request, and candidate-set size such as top-20 versus top-100. Dimension First-stage retrieval Cross-encoder reranking Scoring method Independent encoding + vector similarity / BM25 Joint query-document scoring Speed and scale Very fast; works across large corpora Slower; practical on retrieved candidates only Relevance quality Good for broad recall Better for nuanced final ranking Production role Fetch top-k candidates Reorder top-k into top-n for the LLM Use the practical pattern: retrieve broadly, rerank narrowly. Do not replace scalable retrieval with a cross-encoder over the whole corpus. Use tools like Cohere Rerank or SentenceTransformers cross-encoder models only after fast retrieval proves insufficient on final context quality. How RAG reranking changes precision, recall, latency, and cost Most teams notice the quality problem first and the systems problem later. Better ranking usually helps answer quality, but it also adds one more model call, one more latency source, and one more cost line item. So the real question is not whether reranking helps. It is where it helps, and what it costs. RAG reranking usually helps most with precision at the top of the list . The LLM does not read every retrieved result; it reads only the few chunks that fit into the prompt. If those top 5 or 10 passages are noisy, answer quality can drop even when relevant evidence exists deeper in top-50. Precision goes up first A retrieval reranker -- especially cross-encoder reranking or other model-based reranking -- reorders candidates with more semantic precision than fast first-pass retrieval. In practice, the biggest lift is often in Precision@k , MRR , and nDCG , because the reranker pushes the best evidence closer to rank 1. That is why reranking helps grounded generation: better-ranked context usually means fewer irrelevant chunks in the prompt and less room for the model to improvise. Recall depends on the candidate pool Recall is constrained upstream. A reranker cannot recover a document that never entered the candidate set. If the first stage in a two-stage retrieval pipeline returns only top-10, the reranker can only sort those 10. If the relevant passage sits at rank 24 in Elasticsearch, FAISS, Pinecone, or a hybrid BM25+dense setup, it is already lost. So recall gains usually come indirectly: retrieve a wider pool first, then rerank down to a smaller final set. That can improve Recall@k at the system level, but a too-small top-k caps the upside. Set the retrieval candidate size before choosing the reranker. Otherwise, a strong reranker may have little room to improve results. Latency and cost rise with every extra candidate Longer candidate lists increase reranker latency and inference cost because the model must score more query-document pairs. Longer documents make that worse, and so can a larger model. Track these, at minimum: Precision@k , Recall@k , MRR , or nDCG answer accuracy or grounded answer rate p95 latency throughput cost per query Batching can help. GPU inference is often a better fit for cross-encoders, while CPU placement may be acceptable for lighter models or lower traffic. But concurrency matters: a reranker that looks fine in single-query tests can still become the bottleneck under peak load. A practical rule is to set a latency budget first, then benchmark candidate count, document length, batching, and model size against realistic traffic. That shows whether top-k retrieval alone is enough, or whether reranking earns its extra cost. When top-k retrieval is enough without a retrieval reranker A reranker is easy to justify in theory. In production, the bar should be higher. If the first stage already returns the right evidence near the top, an extra ranking layer may add complexity without changing outcomes. Skip reranking when the first stage is already delivering the right evidence near the top -- consistently, not occasionally. In a production RAG pipeline, top-k retrieval alone is often sufficient when the corpus is small, the language is repetitive, and user queries look like exact match queries or close paraphrases of document text. Internal policy docs, product FAQs, SKU catalogs, and tightly controlled knowledge bases often fit this pattern. In those cases, BM25, Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval, or a strong dense retriever may already produce high candidate quality without cross-encoder reranking . Strict latency budget? That changes the answer fast. If the system must respond in very few milliseconds, a reranker in a two-stage retrieval stack can cost more than it returns. The same applies to low-value interactions where slightly better passage order does not change the final action, answer, or user outcome. A practical rule: measure Precision@k or MRR on real queries before adding complexity. Clarity is better than complexity -- if top-5 results already contain the exact supporting chunk in stable positions, extra ranking is often architectural inflation. Warning signs point the other way. If near-miss passages regularly appear above exact matches, if hybrid retrieval returns broadly relevant but poorly ordered chunks, or if answer quality improves only when humans manually pick better context, reranking is probably justified. Simplicity works only when measured answer quality stays stable under production traffic. How to benchmark whether RAG reranking earns its cost This is where teams can fool themselves. A reranker can look impressive in a demo and still fail the production test because it adds latency, raises cost, or improves ranking metrics without improving answers. The benchmark has to reflect the whole pipeline. Benchmark it as a before-vs-after decision, not a model demo. In a production RAG pipeline, the only useful question is whether RAG reranking improves grounded answers enough to justify extra latency and inference cost. Start with an offline evaluation on a golden dataset of real user queries. Use either relevance judgments at the passage level or answer-level labels such as correct, partially correct, unsupported, and wrong. But do both if possible. Ranking metrics alone can mislead. A cross-encoder reranking layer that improves nDCG or MRR but does not improve final answer quality should not ship. Build the comparison Compare baseline retrieval against retrieval plus reranking under the same prompt and generation settings: first-stage retrieval only two-stage retrieval with cross-encoder reranking same LLM, same prompt, same answer evaluator Measure: retrieval quality: Precision@k, Recall@k, MRR, nDCG answer quality: exactness, groundedness, citation support, human pass rate system impact: p95 latency, token count, reranker cost per query Run an experiment matrix Vary the parts that actually change outcomes: candidate top-k: top-20, top-50, top-100 reranker: Cohere Rerank, SentenceTransformers cross-encoder variants, API vs self-hosted chunking: smaller semantic chunks vs larger fixed windows top-n passed to the LLM: 3, 5, 8 Because understanding why is essential, inspect failure cases -- especially where reranking lifts ranking scores but the answer stays weak. Roll out only if acceptance criteria are met in offline evaluation, then confirm with shadow traffic or an A/B test. A practical gate: require a clear answer-quality lift, no regression on critical query classes, and a bounded p95 latency increase. If the gain is marginal, top-k retrieval alone is usually the better choice. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a cross-encoder and a bi-encoder in retrieval systems? A bi-encoder creates separate embeddings for the query and each document, which makes retrieval fast and scalable across large corpora. A cross-encoder reads the query and document together and outputs a direct relevance score, which is usually more accurate but much slower, so it is best used only on a small retrieved candidate set. How does RAG reranking affect hallucination risk? RAG reranking can reduce hallucination risk by improving the quality of the evidence placed into the prompt, which gives the generator clearer and more directly relevant support. It does not guarantee factual answers, but it lowers the chance that the model anchors on loosely related passages that encourage unsupported synthesis. Why should I benchmark RAG reranking separately from the LLM? You should benchmark RAG reranking separately because a stronger generator can hide retrieval weaknesses, while a weaker one can exaggerate them. Isolating the reranker makes it easier to see whether gains come from better passage ordering or from the answer model itself, which leads to cleaner production decisions. When is RAG reranking usually not worth the cost? RAG reranking is usually not worth the cost when baseline retrieval already places the correct passage in the top few results, query patterns are simple, and latency matters more than marginal quality gains. In those cases, the extra compute, infrastructure, and operational complexity often outweigh the small improvement in final answer quality. Should reranking score full documents or chunks? Reranking should usually score chunks rather than full documents in RAG systems because the generation step consumes compact passages, not long files. Chunk-level scoring gives the reranker a more precise unit of relevance, reduces wasted context window space, and makes it easier to promote the exact evidence the answer needs.

title: Shipping an Embeddable Calculator With No Script Tag, No API and No Build
author: 牛云鹏
summary: Every "add our widget to your site" instruction has quietly become the same thing: paste this <script> , load 180 KB of framework, and let us run code in your page. For a calculator that takes four numbers and does multiplication, that is a bad trade. Here is the version we ship instead, and why each decision went the way it did. One iframe, no script <iframe src= "https://optimetricshub.com/embed/churn" title= "Churn Rate Calculator" width= "100%" height= "700" style= "border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:12px" loading= "lazy" ></iframe> No script tag, no global object, no postMessage handshake, no CORS configuration, nothing added to the embedding page's bundle. The iframe is same-origin to us and cross-origin to you, which means the browser does the isolation for free. Why not a script tag A script tag needs an iframe anyway if you want real isolation. Once you have a <script src> on a third-party page you have inherited: Global namespace collisions. Two analytics widgets both defining window.__widget is a support ticket nobody can reproduce. CSS bleed. Any stylesheet you inject affects the host page. Shadow DOM fixes it, but then you are shipping the shadow-DOM polyfill or accepting a browser floor. A build to maintain. The script is a separate artefact from the page it mirrors, so formulas drift between your site and your embed. Consent and privacy review. A script that reads document.cookie on someone else's domain is a legal conversation. An iframe with no storage access is not. The iframe avoids all four, and costs one extra HTTP request that loading="lazy" mostly defers. Why the arithmetic runs client-side The calculator does not post the numbers anywhere. It computes in the browser and renders the result, which means: No backend to scale. A traffic spike costs nothing. No data-retention question. We cannot lose what we never receive, and the host page's privacy policy does not have to account for us. Instant results. No round trip between keystroke and answer. The trade-off is that the formulas ship to the reader. For a churn or runway calculator that is not a secret worth protecting — the formula is the product. Sizing without a scrollbar The annoying part of iframes is height. A frame that is 40 px too short produces a scrollbar inside a page that already scrolls, which reads as broken. Two options, in order of preference: Fixed heights per embed. Each calculator has a documented height that is slightly above its real content height. It is boring and it never breaks: no JS, no layout shift, no race between content and resize. postMessage + ResizeObserver . Send the content height from inside the frame and set the iframe height on the host. Correct and adaptive, but it needs a script on the host page — which is the thing we were avoiding. We document fixed heights because option 2 undoes the whole design. The heights are in the embed catalogue , along with the snippet for each calculator. The part that is actually load-bearing The frame contains a visible link back to the full tool page. That link is the entire business model: the calculators are free, there is no signup, and the only requirement for embedding is that the attribution stays. This is also why the embed pages are noindex . An embedded copy of a calculator that got indexed would compete with the canonical tool page for the same query, and the site would be cannibalising itself from the inside. What we gave up A widget with postMessage can do things an iframe cannot: push a result into the host page's form, react to the host's theme, participate in the host's state. If you are building a chart library, use a script. If you are building a calculator that takes four numbers, the iframe wins on every axis that matters. title: My WhatsApp Was My Open-Mic Booking System, So I Gave It to Gemma
author: Amrit Dash
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built I'm a stand-up comic in Bangalore, and I curate the Monday and Tuesday open-mic lineups at a club. WhatsApp is my daily driver. I use it to ask other rooms for spots, gossip about shows and audience with comics, reply to my family group, talk to my girlfriend and somewhere in all of that, comics message me asking for a spot on the lineups I curate. Every new message pushes the older ones down. Some requests just slip out of view, and that isn't fair to the comic who asked on Saturday morning. So every week, to keep it fair, I scroll back through every chat, work out who actually asked, check who performed last week (they go to the back of the queue), decide if last week's cancelled mic gets repeated, message everyone, and add and remove people from each show's WhatsApp group by hand. It takes me about 3 hours every week. I'd rather spend those 3 hours writing jokes. Or sleeping. Mostly sleeping. So I built Spot Solutions . A Gemma model running on my old laptop reads my DMs, picks out the real spot requests, and drops them on a lineup board. I drag names into shows, press send, and the confirmations, polite regrets and group updates take care of themselves. Nothing goes out without my OK. I wanted to be lazy, not crazy. Demo Live app: spot-solutions.web.app . Hit Try the live demo and you get your own sandbox of a curator's week. No sign-up. Drag comics around, edit the messages, reset a lineup, break things. It's yours. ( Watch it as a video , 25 seconds.) Here's the weekly loop: Comics DM me like they always have. Nothing changes for them. The server on my laptop waits until a chat goes quiet, then hands the whole burst to Gemma. So "hey" ... "monday?" ... "got a new 5" counts as one request, not three. Gemma decides what each conversation is: a spot request (with preferred days), a cancellation, "am I up this week?", a question about the venue, or noise. Requests land in Waiting on the board. Last week's performers sink to the bottom with a tag. I drag comics into Monday and Tuesday, hit Confirm & send , and review who gets added to and removed from each show's group before anything changes. It's built for the phone, because that's where I actually curate: The Lazy Payoff What Spot Solutions takes off my plate every week: finding the actual requests in a weekend of DMs checking who performed last week, who asked for which day, and whether a cancelled mic repeats messaging every comic, the ones who got a spot and the ones who didn't adding and removing people from each show's group Before: about 3 hours a week. Now: about 15 minutes , most of it spent dragging names around. That's about 12 hours a month back. It also runs for next to nothing, on a laptop that was gathering dust. This isn't my first attempt either. Version 1 ran for 7 months across 2024 and 2025 on Google Apps Script, Google Sheets and Twilio: 2,200+ spot requests from 150+ comics. It worked, but it needed rigid keywords, cost money per message, and every rule lived in spreadsheet formulas. Version 2 keeps all the rules V1 learned (request windows, skip-last-week, ban and ignore lists, "did the mic happen?" checks, last-minute spot offers) and lets Gemma handle the messy human part. How I Built It WhatsApp: whatsapp-web.js in a Node worker. One headless WhatsApp Web session per curator. AI: Gemma 3 (4B) through Ollama , on the same laptop. Gemini is an optional fallback, off unless you add a key. App: React + Vite with Material 3, hosted on Firebase. Works on a phone, and installs as a PWA. The glue: Firestore. The web app writes commands, the worker listens and writes results back. The laptop only makes outbound connections. No open ports, no tunnel, no static IP. It works on home Wi-Fi while I'm on mobile data across town. The part where the small model broke Comics ask for spots in every way imaginable: "bhai monday ka spot milega? naya 5 hai" "put me down pls" "any day works, got new bits" "guru tuesday sigutta?" And my WhatsApp isn't only comics. It's bank alerts, UPI receipts, OTPs, delivery updates, forwarded memes and audience members asking about tickets. A 4B model asked "is this a spot request?" will say yes with confidence to things that clearly aren't, and a confidence score alone didn't protect against that. What worked was making the model quote the ask . Every classification has to include an evidence field copied from the messages, and the worker checks that quote is really there: /** The model must quote the ask. If its "evidence" isn't actually in the messages, it made it up. */ export function evidenceIsReal ( evidence : string , messages : string []) { const ev = norm ( evidence ); if ( ! ev ) return false ; const text = norm ( messages . join ( " " )); if ( text . includes ( ev )) return true ; const words = ev . split ( " " ). filter (( w ) => w . length > 1 ); const hits = words . filter (( w ) => text . includes ( w )). length ; return words . length > 0 && hits / words . length >= 0.75 ; } If the quote isn't in the chat, the classification gets thrown out as noise. The model can't invent a request out of a bank alert when it has to point at the words. The 75% word match is loose on purpose: Hinglish has no fixed spelling, so a quote can drift a little from the original and still be honest. Auto-acknowledging ("got your request, will confirm soon") is off by default. When it's on, it needs a quoted ask at 85%+ confidence, in a message under 10 minutes old, from a real person and never a business account. Making an old laptop a real server Most of the second half of the week went into making the server boring to run: One installer each for Ubuntu (even from a USB stick), Windows and macOS. The Mac gets a small menu-bar app. It survives restarts, power cuts and closed lids. The WhatsApp login gets backed up, and when the server comes back it catches up on DMs that arrived while it was down, without auto-replying to any of them. Restarting the worker, restarting Ollama, reading logs and approving new curators all happen from the app's Server page, so after setup I never need to touch the laptop. It's invite-only. Other curators sign in, I approve them, and they link their own WhatsApp. An 8 GB laptop should comfortably host about 6 curators. Why Open Matters Here My comics' DMs are private. People send me their phone numbers, their sets, their bad days. Sending every one of those messages to a cloud API so a model can decide whether "bro monday?" is a spot request felt wrong. With Gemma running locally: No cloud model reads the chats. Gemma reads them on my own laptop, and messages that aren't spot requests aren't even stored. The AI costs nothing. No per-message bill, which matters when a busy weekend means hundreds of messages. I can swap the model. Gemma 3 1B on a weak machine, 12B on a better one, or Gemini as a fallback when I choose. Each curator gets a setting for this: "Local only" or "Local first". Old hardware gets a second life. The laptop running this was headed for a drawer. And it's all MIT licensed. Another open-mic scene can run its own server for its own comics, and nothing about it depends on me. Several Laptops, One Lineup One laptop is a single point of failure, and old laptops fail. So Spot Solutions runs on as many servers as you want, all pointed at the same project: a Mac, a Windows laptop, an Ubuntu box in a cupboard. Each WhatsApp account runs on exactly one of them at a time. That server holds a lease and renews it every 30 seconds. If it goes quiet (power cut, closed lid, a cat on the keyboard), it stops its own WhatsApp first, and only after that can another server take the account over. The new server doesn't ask for a QR scan. It pulls an encrypted copy of the WhatsApp login from Cloud Storage, unlocks it, and carries on. Every copy gets a version number, and the newest copy always wins, so a laptop that comes back after a week can't overwrite a fresher login with its old one. Accounts go to the least busy server, curators can pin themselves to one, and a curator who picks "Local only" only ever lands on a server running Gemma. Each machine gets its own key, so if a laptop gets stolen I revoke that one key and the rest keep running. Code amrit-contour / spot-solutions Open-mic lineup curation on autopilot: WhatsApp spot requests triaged by local Gemma, a lineup board, and a server that runs on any old laptop. Spot Solutions Open-mic lineup curation on autopilot. Comics DM you for spots on WhatsApp; a local Gemma model works out who's actually asking, acknowledges them, and drops them into a dashboard where you drag names into shows and hit send. Everyone who didn't make it gets a polite regret, and each show's WhatsApp group is updated to match the lineup. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 3: Slow and Steady ). How it works Web app (React, Firebase Hosting) ──▶ Firestore ◀── Worker on your laptop Google sign-in, lineup board realtime whatsapp-web.js (1 session / curator) writes commands + config uid-scoped Ollama · gemma3:4b (Gemini API fallback) The worker only makes outbound connections. No ports, no tunnel. The web app drops commands into Firestore and the worker executes them. Intake: inbound DMs are debounced per chat (45s), so "hey" … "monday?" … "got a new 5"… View on GitHub Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 runs every AI decision in the app, locally through Ollama: reading bursts of Hinglish, English and Kannada DMs, sorting them into spot requests, cancellations, questions and noise, pulling out preferred days, and quoting the ask so nothing gets invented. Curators who pick "Local only" never touch a cloud model at all. Built with Gemma 3, Ollama, whatsapp-web.js, React and Firebase, mostly by a sloth with a laptop and a AI subscription.

In local mode, data lives only in the SQLite file on your own computer — zero telemetry, and no requests are sent to any server; In cloud sync mode, Supabase's top-tier PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) enforces at the database layer that only your own credentials can access that row — even a backend administrator cannot view your bookmarks. Q4: Compared with the browser's built-in bookmark bar, what is Linkit's biggest improvement? A: From "passive hoarding" to "active empowerment." Traditional browser bookmarks are flat dead links: they can't record reading state (unread / reading / read), can't search page content, and dead links and duplicates accumulate without end. Linkit turns every web page into a knowledge asset with state, tags, a summary, and associations , and pairs it with quick search and periodic insight reports — genuinely turning fragmented internet knowledge into your own capability. 🌟 Experience Linkit Today and Start a Cleaner Knowledge Management Journey Don't let precious ideas and knowledge keep sleeping in a chaotic collection!
