title: Design full test-space scenarios at once and delegate precised evidence-based exploratory testing to your AI
author: Yurii Baranov
summary: You Can’t List Your Unknown Bugs, but You Can Model What Varies. Combinatorics-Framework-JVM turns a model of settings, action histories and optional events into planned test cases, and keeps the experiment inspectable from design through evidence. ⚡️ Straight to the point for most impatient/busy-reader who respects human's work (let your AI read 'AI_DELEGATION.md' after dowloading the release, and it will answer you live): Combinatorics-Framework-JVM “What kinds of bugs does my system under test have?” It sounds like the obvious first question for any testing tool. It’s also the wrong one. If you could answer it, you’d already have the tests. The defects that hurt are the ones nobody knew to name: a guest, a coupon and a repeated payment request, each fine alone and wrong together. AI coding assistants sharpen the problem. An assistant can implement the feature, generate the unit tests and explain why the code should work. It can’t tell you which interactions those tests exercised. So don’t start from bugs. Start from three questions you can answer: What varies? Settings, inputs, the order of actions, events that may or may not happen. What must stay true? An invariant, such as “the same payment request creates at most one charge.” How much am I willing to run? A bounded budget of cases you can actually inspect. Bugs aren’t the input to that exercise. They’re the output. Investigation, not diagnosis Combinatorics-Framework-JVM is built for exactly that kind of investigational testing: a Java workbench with a desktop app (guif), a command line and an embedding API. You describe the variations, it generates test candidates, runs them through your configured runners and helps you examine the results. State a model, run a bounded experiment, read the evidence, refine the model, repeat. It won’t discover unknown defects for you. It turns a test idea into a visible model, a bounded run and results another engineer can inspect. Model the context, and the history Take a small checkout: What varies Choices Customer Guest, registered Payment method Card, wallet, cash on delivery Channel Website, API Pricing policy Current price, price captured earlier That’s 24 static combinations. Run them all. Now add history: submit, time out, retry, a price change at different moments. The input values barely changed. The history did, and no parameter table shows it. So the Framework models three kinds of variation separately: Static context: account type, payment method, feature flags. Covering selection can reduce this part to a declared interaction strength. Action sequences: what happens first, next and again, including order and repetition. Sudden or optional events: a timeout, a duplicate request, a price change, including when it strikes and the case where it never does. Sequences and sudden events are then crossed with every selected context, not squeezed into the same matrix. That stops you from flattening everything into interchangeable parameters and assuming you tested the histories that matter. For a workflow bug, the timeline deserves more attention than a big parameter matrix. Constraints need the same care. An impossible combination can be excluded. A valid input the application should reject (cash on delivery over the API, say) deserves a negative test, not a deletion. The modeler decides which question a test answers. The generator can’t. A model you can read in one minute Two modes, three actions. Every candidate gets one mode and two different actions in a chosen order (AB, BA, AC, CA, BC, CB): 2 × 6 = 12 candidates. Save this as first-scenario.json : { "spec_version" : "1" , "title" : "Two modes and ordered pairs of actions" , "slots" : [ { "sheet" : "MODE" , "alias" : "choose_one" , "raw" : true , "values" : [ "safe" , "fast" ] }, { "sheet" : "OPS" , "alias" : "permute(2)" , "flags" : [ "FW_Concatenator=" ], "raw" : true , "values" : [ "A" , "B" , "C" ] } ] } And these settings as first-scenario.properties : cf.coverage.strength = 0 cf.coverage.budget = 0 cf.plan.autoPromoteSingleVerb = true Then, with JDK 25 and fw-app.jar in your working folder: java -Djava .awt.headless = true -jar fw-app.jar validate --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties java -Djava .awt.headless = true -jar fw-app.jar plan --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties java -Djava .awt.headless = true -jar fw-app.jar candidates --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties --limit 12 Validate, inspect the plan, read the candidates, all before anything runs. These are plain-text candidates for learning the model, not programs to execute. Prefer spreadsheets? The classic workbook style (data sheets plus an FW_Seq control sheet) expresses the same model, and the wizard in guif guides a first scenario. When order is the bug A basic retry test submits a request twice with the same key and confirms that one order exists. Now change the history: the provider accepts the first request, its response times out, a confirmation arrives while the client is retrying, and the client tries again. Is there still exactly one charge and one order? A small timeline model might include these histories: History Events the harness controls A Submit → success → retry the same request B Submit → timeout → retry → confirmation C Submit → timeout → confirmation → retry D Submit → timeout → retry → retry → confirmation The invariant: reusing a request key must never create a second charge or a second order. Check durable business state (charges, orders, how they relate), not just the final HTTP status. One honest boundary: the Framework generates ordered choices, permutations, repetitions and optional events. It doesn’t control a thread scheduler or a remote payment provider. Your adapter has to make those events controllable: hold and release a callback, simulate a timeout, reset state. Once it does, you vary the histories without hand-copying a test method for every combination. A planted defect, caught (quick self-test) You don’t have to take this on faith. The project’s manual ships a self-contained checkout demo whose stand-in system has a deliberately planted lost-order defect. validate , plan and candidates report 72 generated cases, 24 removed by one constraint and 48 executable. The full run ends with 44 PASS and 4 DOMAIN_FAIL, with no harness failures. The repo’s validation report records this on JDK 25 and a 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT build. A larger showcase in the manual runs 4,128 generated Cucumber scenarios against an in-JVM checkout engine and 714 browser scenarios (Selenium, headless Firefox) against a dummy web shop, both with planted defects hiding in action order and event timing. A second run of each design gave the same verdict for every case. Two things to notice: A run that finds defects still exits with code 0. A failure is a result, not a crash, so read the verdicts. Keep product failures (DOMAIN_FAIL) apart from harness outcomes such as BROKEN, TIMEOUT and INFRA_FAIL. Every defect here was planted. That shows the harness can see a fault, not that it finds ones nobody knows about. It’s why the manual says to calibrate the oracle with a known-failing case before trusting a model. The unknown bugs are what the experiment is for. What comes back Failures arrive as cases, not red lights: the candidate, its verdict, its measurements and the context to reproduce it. Checkpoints and exports keep the evidence, and triage groups failures into findings with representative witnesses. The documented “minimal witness” is the failing case with the least source in its group: a good place to start, not a proven mathematical minimum. Values associated with elevated failure rates are leads, not causes. When nothing fails, you still get something: “within this model, at this strength, no violation observed.” That isn’t proof of absence. It’s a claim another engineer can inspect, challenge and extend. What you bring, and what it doesn’t promise The Framework generates and organizes. You make it real. The model and the invariant are yours: it doesn’t discover what must stay true (a far easier question than “what is broken?”, but not a free one). You also bring: An adapter that connects candidates to your system and controls its state and dependencies. An oracle: assertions that encode the invariant. A generated case without a meaningful check is just activity. A controlled environment with a reset strategy, plus the judgment about which failures matter and what went untested. And be honest about the limits: Pairwise isn’t magic. It covers pairs of modeled values, not every three-way defect, action order or timing failure, and the selection is greedy, so it never claims a minimum suite. With fewer than three varying factors, every pair is already the whole space and nothing is reduced. Its value is that you can state what you selected and inspect it. One verdict per case. The first failing check names the verdict and hides later ones, so report every check as a metric too. No OS sandbox for Java. Java cases run inside the Framework’s own JVM with your permissions, so treat every run as code execution on your machine: use a dedicated workspace and keep production out until the adapter, assertions and side effects are clear. Python cases run as separate processes and can be sandboxed with bwrap or Docker. The same machinery, for AI experiments Prompts × retrieval strategies × thresholds is a combinatorial space too. Three retrieval strategies, two prompts and two thresholds make 12 configurations. Evaluate each on 50 questions, twice: 1,200 evaluations, not 12. Mind that arithmetic when a provider bills per request. Multi-goal analysis, including a Pareto front, keeps cost and quality trade-offs visible instead of collapsing them into one early score. It describes what you measured, not the best system that could exist. Bring an evaluation method you trust, because there is no universal judge of LLM answers, and test the evaluator with a deliberately wrong answer. Generation is deterministic; a remote model isn’t, so record versions, settings and rate limits. Hand your assistant an experiment, not a vibe The model and the recorded evidence are files, so a second engineer, or a later assistant session, can pick them up without reconstructing a chat. Give your assistant evidence, not a symptom: Here is the failing candidate (submit → timeout → retry → confirmation) and the two charge IDs it returned. The invariant is one request key, at most one charge. Propose a mechanism that fits this evidence, a focused change, and which existing cases would distinguish your explanation from the alternatives. That asks for a testable claim instead of a guessed fix. Then rerun the same candidate and its surrounding histories against the change: if a repair fixes one sequence and breaks another, the regression stays visible. The repo is built for this hand-off. The manual, AI_DELEGATION.md , is written for an AI operator acting for a human supervisor, and the desktop’s AI_delegation button copies its path for you to paste. Copying a path isn’t consent. The manual’s first rule is no agreement, no operation : the assistant needs your explicit yes, then must ask before it finalizes the design, executes any case (a smoke run comes first), builds or installs anything, or touches the network, files outside the agreed workspace or your system under test. It must report what it did and didn’t check, and never present a plausible explanation as an observed result. You stay the director, and the license makes that a condition. Try it small Pick a behavior you already understand, ideally a defect you’ve already fixed. Write three or four factors, one troublesome sequence and one invariant. Stay small enough to preview every candidate, and change one thing at a time. Inject a fault into a local implementation. Does the scenario catch it? Fix it and rerun. Save the scenario, run ID, checkpoint and evidence. If you can express the behavior, understand the generated cases and recognize a useful failure, it fits. The manual itself rates a few situations as poor fits: one or two parameters, purely continuous spaces, no reliable oracle, and state you can’t reset. Use unit or property tests, fuzzing or an optimizer there, and keep the plain unit test whenever it already pins a defect down. Reach for a scenario model when the variations themselves are getting hard to track. Requirements, status and license First of all: AS IS..., no warranty Requirements: JDK 25, a full JDK with the compiler rather than a bare JRE, because generated cases are compiled in memory. The core workflow needs no Python, no relational database and no containers. Python 3.11+ and the Python add-on are optional, for Python candidates. Status: first public release (Oct 2026), one maintainer. It’s early-stage, so validate it on your own workload before it carries anything critical. The case for it is specific. Interacting settings, action sequences and timed events get one shared model, the model becomes inspectable candidates, and the results stay available for review and retesting. For the bugs that live between individually working features, and for AI-assisted work that needs evidence rather than confidence, that’s worth a small trial. Don’t ask it where your bugs are. Tell it what varies and what must stay true, then read what comes back. P.S. You are a Scenario Test-space Architect/Designer (puzzle-items of any kind) and a supervisor of AI (who operates on "Combinatorics Framework" as a precise tool for all of these) 🧩🧩🧩🧩🧩 GitHub project and downloads

title: ElevenLabs API key: free tier tested on 4 models, incl. v4 and Vietnamese
author: RanThis
summary: An ElevenLabs API key works on the free plan, and it is enough to try every current text-to-speech model, including Eleven v4. We created one with a 2,000-credit cap and ran the same sentence through four models in English and Vietnamese, then hit the free plan's walls on purpose to see the exact errors. Below: how the key behaves, what each call cost in credits, how fast it was, and what the free tier blocks. Measured on 24 Oct 2026 with one key on an ElevenLabs Free account, from a Python script on a Windows 11 PC (WSL, Ubuntu 24.04) in Vietnam. Prices are from ElevenLabs' pricing pages, read the same day. Key results The free key ran all four models we tried : Flash v2.5, Multilingual v2, v3 and the new v4. Each call returned a 128 kbps MP3 of about 8–9 seconds for a 140-character sentence. Flash cost half. A 140-character sentence cost 70 credits on Flash v2.5 and 140 on the other three. The API says so in a character-cost response header on every call. The usage counter lags. Right after eight calls, /v1/user/subscription still showed 0 credits used; a few minutes later it showed 1,050, exactly the sum of the headers. Pick the model by language. Played back through ElevenLabs' own speech-to-text, Vietnamese from Flash v2.5, v3 and v4 came back word for word; Multilingual v2, which does not list Vietnamese, came back garbled (61% word error rate). Streaming is fast. Flash v2.5 over the streaming endpoint sent its first audio bytes in 0.19 s and finished in 0.40 s. The free tier blocks three things we tried : 192 kbps MP3 (Creator and up), 44.1 kHz PCM (Pro and up) and voices from the community library (Creator and up). The 21 default voices work. Setup Account: ElevenLabs Free, 10,000 credits a month, no payment method. Key: created on 24 Oct 2026 in the ElevenLabs web app under Developers → API Keys, with a 2,000-credit limit and no expiry. It sits in an .env file on the server that runs the script, never in a browser. Client: Python 3.13 with httpx , calling https://api.elevenlabs.io directly with the xi-api-key header (no SDK). Voice: "Bella", the first of the 21 default voices the key could list. Text: one sentence of 140 characters in English and one of 140 characters in Vietnamese, the same meaning in both. Checks: credits from the character-cost header and from /v1/user/subscription ; timing from the start of the request to the last byte; Vietnamese accuracy by sending each file to /v1/speech-to-text ( scribe_v1 ) and comparing the transcript with the original sentence. Audio length is estimated from file size at 128 kbps. How to get an ElevenLabs API key Sign in to ElevenLabs (a free account is enough). Open Developers → API Keys and create a key. Give it a name per app, and set the limits ElevenLabs offers: which endpoints the key can call, a credit quota, and an IP allowlist. We set a 2,000-credit quota so a bug in the script could not drain the month's 10,000 credits. Store it as an environment variable ( ELEVENLABS_API_KEY ) on your server. Send it in an xi-api-key header on every request. A first test call is GET /v1/models , which lists the models your key can use. ElevenLabs' docs say plainly that the key is a secret and should not go into client-side code such as browsers or apps. For calls that must come from the client, the docs point to single-use tokens instead. What the API told us when the key was wrong: Request Status Message No key 401 "Neither authorization header nor xi-api-key received, please provide one." Wrong key 401 "Invalid API key" Our key 200 Subscription details: tier free , 10,000-credit limit What each model cost and how fast it was Same voice, same 140-character sentence, one call each, full MP3 returned (not streamed): Model Credits (EN / VI) Time to full file, EN Time to full file, VI Audio length Flash v2.5 70 / 70 2.04 s* 0.36 s ~8.7 s / ~7.5 s Multilingual v2 140 / 140 1.43 s 1.48 s ~8.9 s / ~9.1 s v3 140 / 140 2.67 s 3.17 s ~8.4 s / ~8.4 s v4 140 / 140 2.51 s 2.35 s ~9.2 s / ~8.9 s *The first call of the run, which included opening the connection; the Vietnamese Flash call right after took 0.36 s. On the streaming endpoint ( /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id}/stream ), Flash v2.5 delivered the first bytes of the English sentence in 0.19 s and the whole file in 0.40 s. That is the number that matters for anything that talks back to a user. The /v1/models list explains the credits: Flash, Turbo, v4 Turbo and v3 Conversational carry a 0.5 character-cost multiplier, the rest 1.0. It also shows the per-request ceiling on the free plan: 40,000 characters for Flash v2.5, 10,000 for v4 and Multilingual v2, 5,000 for v3. Which models speak Vietnamese We fed each Vietnamese file to ElevenLabs' speech-to-text and compared what came back with what we sent. Model Vietnamese in its language list Word error rate What came back Flash v2.5 yes 6.5% Identical except "khoá" spelled "khóa" (both are correct spellings) v3 yes 6.5% Same as Flash v4 yes 6.5% Same, but the first word heard as "Khoa" Multilingual v2 no 61.3% Mostly garbled: "giống như mật khẩu" became "Gyeonghu mắt kháu" So the 6.5% for the first three is spelling, not pronunciation. Multilingual v2 still returns audio and charges full credits for a language it does not support, without an error. Check a model's languages in /v1/models before you choose it. A machine transcript is not a native listener. It catches words the model got wrong, not how natural the voice sounds. What the free key cannot do What we tried Result output_format=mp3_44100_192 403: "Output format 'mp3_44100_192' is only available on the Creator tier and above." output_format=pcm_44100 403: "Output format 'pcm_44100' is only available on the Pro tier and above." A voice from the community voice library 400: "You need to be on the creator tier or above to use this voice." Instant voice cloning Not tried; the subscription response reports can_use_instant_voice_cloning: false Failed requests did not use credits. The 21 default voices and 128 kbps MP3 all worked. The subscription response also lists a limit of 3 custom voices on our free account. The other limit is the licence. On ElevenLabs' pricing page the Commercial License is listed from the Starter plan up, not on Free, so a free key is for building and testing. What it costs after the free credits Plan or billing Price Credits or characters Free $0 10,000 credits a month, no rollover Starter $6 a month (a $1 first month was on offer until 1 Nov when we checked) 30,000 credits a month, commercial licence Creator $22 a month ($11 the first month) 121,000 credits a month API, pay as you go $0.08 per 1,000 characters on v4, v3 and Multilingual v2; $0.04 on Flash/Turbo billed in dollars, not credits Prices exclude tax, according to the pricing page. At the Flash rate our 140-character sentence costs well under a cent: $0.04 per 1,000 characters is about $0.0056 for 140. What worked One environment variable and a header: the first request worked without an SDK. The character-cost header gave an exact cost per call immediately, which the subscription endpoint did not. The per-key credit cap is a cheap safety net. Ours capped the test at 2,000 of the month's 10,000 credits. Every limit we hit came back with a readable message that names the plan you need. What didn't work The usage counter was not real-time. If you meter your own users from /v1/user/subscription , you will undercount; read the response header instead. Multilingual v2 accepted Vietnamese text and charged full price for unusable audio. One sentence per model is enough to spot a broken language, not to rank voice quality. We did not run long texts, many voices or a listening test. Our verdict If you want to try ElevenLabs from code, a free API key is enough: it runs the newest model, v4, and the cheap Flash model, returns usable 128 kbps audio, and its limits are clear. Put a credit cap on the key, keep it server-side, and log the character-cost header rather than trusting the usage counter. For a language other than English, check that it is in the model's list first: Flash v2.5 was the cheapest and fastest model that read our Vietnamese correctly. Pay when you need commercial use, higher-quality formats or library voices. Frequently asked questions Is the ElevenLabs API key free? Yes. A free account can create API keys and uses the plan's 10,000 monthly credits. On Flash v2.5 that was 0.5 credits per character in our test. Where do I find my ElevenLabs API key? In the ElevenLabs web app under Developers → API Keys. You can create several keys and limit each one by endpoints, credits and IP addresses. How do I use the ElevenLabs API key? Send it in an xi-api-key header, for example on GET https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/models . Keep it on a server; ElevenLabs says not to put it in browser or app code. Can I use ElevenLabs v4 with a free API key? In our test, yes: Eleven v4 returned audio on a free key and cost 1 credit per character. Can I use the free ElevenLabs API commercially? ElevenLabs' pricing page lists the Commercial License from the Starter plan up, not on Free. Original article with the full tables and sources: https://ranthis.com/guides/elevenlabs-api-key

title: Why I Stopped Paying for ElevenLabs in 2026: The Hidden Limitations for Commercial Video Workflows
author: zrr
summary: A transparent look at character caps, overage pricing shocks, and why deterministic neural engines took over my daily production. Let me state this upfront: ElevenLabs is technically brilliant. Their generative voice cloning models set the industry standard for short-form realism, dramatic range, and conversational warmth. If you are producing 30-second character skits or indie video game dialogue, their technology is unmatched. However, after 10 months of running an active commercial video production pipeline—producing YouTube explainer series, technical tutorials, and long-form narrations—I recently cancelled my paid subscription. It wasn't because the audio sounded robotic. It was because the platform’s business model and architecture create severe friction the moment you scale past hobbyist clips. Here is the honest production reality behind why generative voice subscriptions break down for high-volume video workflows, and what I switched to instead. 1. The "Overage Tax" and Failed Render Burn ElevenLabs charges on a monthly character quota (e.g., ~100,000 characters on the Creator tier). On paper, 100,000 characters sounds generous (roughly 1.5 to 2 hours of audio). In a real production environment, you never render text once: You adjust a sentence for better pacing → quota burned twice . The generative model hallucinates a whisper or slurs a proper noun at minute four → full paragraph re-rendered, quota burned again . You revise your video script based on client feedback → quota burned a third time . In practice, rendering a clean 20-minute video master track typically consumes 3x the character count of the actual script . Once you exceed your monthly quota, automatic overage fees kick in. I frequently found myself burning through a $22 tier within the first 10 days of the month, turning monthly audio expenses into an unpredictable $60–$90 variable cost. 2. Acoustic Inconsistency Across Long Scripts Generative autoregressive models predict audio token by token. This produces wonderful emotional nuance, but it has a dark side: non-determinism . If you render a 3,000-word narration in sections: Section 1 sounds energetic and forward; Section 2 sounds intimate and slightly hushed; Section 3 introduces subtle vocal frying. When spliced together on an editing timeline, the tonal shifts become jarringly obvious through studio headphones. To get a cohesive take, creators spend hours manually cherry-picking seeds—completely defeating the point of automated voice generation. 3. The Reverse Subtitle Dilemma When producing video content, audio is only 50% of the deliverable. You must have synchronized subtitles ( .srt ). Because black-box generative APIs output a flat .mp3 with zero word-boundary telemetry, you are forced to pipe that rendered audio back into an AI transcription engine (like Whisper) just to recover the timestamps you already owned in your source manuscript. It adds extra render steps, introduces Whisper transcription hallucinations on quiet breaths, and doubles your processing latency. The Pivot to Deterministic Neural Workbenches For serious video creators and instructional designers, raw "vocal flair" matters far less than consistency, predictability, and friction-free editing . Over the last few months, my daily production has transitioned almost entirely to browser-level workbenches built on Microsoft Azure’s Speech Core (such as the free VoiceIndex Studio ): Production Factor Generative Subscriptions (ElevenLabs) Deterministic Workbenches (Azure / VoiceIndex) Pricing Model $22+/mo with hard character caps Free / Transparent Pay-per-use Long-Form Consistency Tonal drift between takes 100% Deterministic & Fatigue-Free Setup Friction Mandatory account & credit card Zero-signup instant browser export Subtitle Synchronization Post-process Whisper pass required Native millisecond .srt output Pacing Control Sliders with random seeds Precision W3C SSML breaks & prosody Voices like en-US-RyanNeural , en-US-JennyNeural , and zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural may not sound like Shakespearean actors, but they deliver crisp, professional, fatigue-free audio that never drifts in tone, never charges surprise overages, and exports synchronized subtitles instantly. Summary: Matching the Tool to the Job Stick with ElevenLabs if : You produce short fiction, voice acting, gaming characters, or require high-stakes zero-shot voice cloning. Switch to Deterministic Neural Tools if : You produce high-volume commercial video essays, tutorials, audiobooks, or documentation where predictable costs, zero setup friction, and instant subtitle synchronization determine your profit margins. Are you currently using generative voice platforms or deterministic neural tools for your long-form video projects? Have you run into character quota burn during revisions? Share your workflow in the responses.
